I shall practise all this rightly, Janardana. And this was done most marvellously out of a wish to please us:
mahabharata:14:51.18	that the sinful Kaurava, Dhritarashtra's son, was slain in battle. That army was burned by you; I conquered it in the fight.
mahabharata:14:51.19	That deed done by you is how victory over Duryodhana in the war was won by me, by your wisdom and valour.
mahabharata:14:51.20	The way to kill Karna was shown rightly, and of the sinful Saindhava and of Bhurishravas as well.
mahabharata:14:51.21	And I, pleased with you, son of Devaki, will do what you have said; of that there is no doubt.
mahabharata:14:51.22	And approaching the righteous King Yudhishthira, knower of dharma, I shall urge him about your going, blameless one.
mahabharata:14:51.23	This going of yours to Dvaraka pleases me, lord; before long you will see your maternal uncle, Madhusudana, and the invincible Baladeva and the other Vrishni bulls.
Speaking so, the two reached Varanasahvaya and entered the city, crowded with delighted people.
Going to Dhritarashtra's house, like the house of Shakra, the two saw, O great king, Dhritarashtra, lord of men,
and the greatly wise Vidura, King Yudhishthira, the invincible Bhimasena, Madri's two Pandava sons, and the unconquered Yuyutsu attending Dhritarashtra,
and the greatly wise Gandhari, Pritha and the lovely Krishna; and Subhadra and all the Bharata women standing around Gandhari.
Then the two scourges of foes, meeting King Dhritarashtra, announced their names and took his feet.
So too the two great souls took the feet of Gandhari, Pritha, the king of dharma and Bhima.
Having honoured Kshatta too and asked after his imperishable well-being, they then attended the aged king with them.
Then at night, O great king, the wise Dhritarashtra dismissed the Kuru heroes and Janardana to their houses.
Given leave by the king, they went each to his own dwelling; Dhananjaya went to his own house, and the mighty Krishna with him.
There, honoured as is fit and supplied with all desires, the wise Krishna slept, with Dhananjaya at his side.
When the night had passed and they had done their forenoon rites, the two went, greatly honoured, to the house of Dharmaraja, where the great-minded king of dharma sat with his ministers.
Entering, the two mighty ones saw Dharmaraja seated like the king of the gods with the two Ashvins.
Approaching the king, Vrishni and the bull of the Kurus sat down with his leave, and he was pleased.
Then that wise king, best of kings and best of speakers, seeing that the two wished to speak, said:
I think you two, heroes of the Yadus and Kurus, wish to say something. Speak; I shall do it all for you without delay; do not hesitate.
Thus addressed, Phalguna, skilled in speech, approached the king of dharma humbly and said:

This mighty Vasudeva, king, has stayed a long time; with your leave he wishes to see his father.
mahabharata:14:51.41	He should go, given leave by you, if you think so; you should give leave to the hero for the city of Anarta.
[Yudhishthira] "Lotus-eyed one, good fortune to you; go today, Madhusudana, to the city of Dvaravati to see your father, the lord Shurasena's son.
Your going pleases me, mighty-armed Keshava; I have not seen for long my maternal uncle, and the goddess Devaki, with you.
Madhava, greatly wise one, honour my uncle Vasudeva and Baladeva as is fit, in my name.
And always remember me, and Bhima, the best of the strong, Phalguna, Nakula and Sahadeva, Madhava.
Having seen the Anartas and your father, mighty-armed one, and the Vrishnis, blameless one, come again to my horse sacrifice.
Go, taking jewels and many kinds of wealth, and take whatever else pleases you, Satvata.
For by your grace, Madhava, this whole earth has come to us, hero, and our enemies have been slain."
When the Kaurava Yudhishthira, king of dharma, said this, Vasudeva, best of men, spoke these words.
The jewels and wealth, and the whole earth, mighty-armed one, are yours alone today; and whatever other property is in my houses, you alone are lord of it, always the lord.
So addressed and honoured, "So be it," the mighty elder brother of Gada, honoured by Dharma's son, greeted his father's sister by rule and, honoured, circled her and went.
Rightly welcomed by her and by Vidura and all the others, Hari, Gada's elder brother, left Nagapura in a divine four-horse chariot.
Placing the lovely Subhadra in the chariot with Yudhishthira's leave and his father's sister, the mighty-armed Janardana departed, surrounded by townspeople.
He was followed by the one with the ape banner, by Satyaki, by Madri's two sons, by the deep-minded Vidura, and by Bhima himself, with an elephant king's valour.
Having sent back all the increasers of the Kuru realm and Vidura, the mighty Janardana quickly said to Daruka, "Urge on the horses," and then to Satyaki.
Then Janardana, crusher of hosts of enemies, followed by Shini's heroic grandson, went to the city of Anarta, as Shatakratu goes to heaven having slain his enemy hosts.
Again and again Phalguna embraced Vrishni, and looked at him until he was out of sight, and again and again.
With difficulty Partha drew back his gaze fixed on Govinda, and the unconquered Krishna did so too.
At the great soul's departure there were many omens of marvellous kind; hear them as I tell.
A wind blew in front of the chariot with great speed, making the road free of gravel, dust and thorns.
Vasava also rained pure, fragrant water, and divine flowers fell before the bearer of the Sharnga bow.
The mighty-armed one set out, and on the level deserts saw the best of sages, Uttanka, of immeasurable power.
The radiant, wide-eyed one honoured that sage, and honoured by him he then asked about his health.
Asked about his well-being by Krishna, Uttanka, best of brahmins, honoured Madhusudana and then asked Madhava:

Have you returned, Keshava, having reconciled those heroes, your dearest kinsmen, ever, bull of the Vrishnis?
mahabharata:14:52.12	Will the five sons of Pandu and the sons of Dhritarashtra sport in the worlds with you, scourge of foes?
mahabharata:14:52.13	Will kings in their own realms gain happiness, the Kauravas being at peace, with you as lord, Madhava?
mahabharata:14:52.14	The hope I always had in you, dear one, has it come true in what you did for the Bharatas, Krishna?
[Vasudeva] "I made an effort, brahmin, for good brotherhood with the Kauravas, but those lovers of unrighteousness could not be reconciled by me.
Then they all met their end with sons and kinsmen. Fate cannot be passed beyond by intellect or strength, great sage; surely you know all this, blameless one.
They transgressed my counsel, and Bhishma's and Vidura's, and went to Yama's abode, attacking one another.
Five Pandavas remain, their friends and sons slain, and the Dhritarashtras were all slain with sons and kinsmen."
When Krishna had said this, Uttanka, filled with great anger, rolling his eyes in rage, replied to him:

Because, Krishna, though able you did not save the Kurus and Pandavas, your dear kinsmen, I shall curse you, without doubt.
mahabharata:14:52.21	Because you did not forcibly restrain them and turn them back, I, seized by anger, shall curse you, Madhusudana.
mahabharata:14:52.22	For you, though able, by false conduct, Madhava, allowed these best of the Kurus to be ruined, who disregarded them.
[Vasudeva] "Hear this at length, joy of the Bhrigus, what I shall tell, and accept my appeasement, for you are an ascetic, Bhargava.
Having heard this spiritual teaching, you should release the curse today, and no man can overcome me by little austerity.
I do not wish to destroy your austerity, best of those who mutter prayers; your austerity is greatly blazing and your teachers are pleased.
I know your celibacy from boyhood, best of brahmins; therefore I do not wish to waste your austerity won with pain."
[Vasudeva] "Know darkness, passion and goodness as states dependent on me, and know the Rudras and Vasus, brahmin, as born of me.
All beings are in me and I am in all beings; know this; let there be no doubt in you here.
So too know the hosts of daityas, yakshas, rakshasas and serpents, and gandharvas and apsarases, brahmin, as born of me.
Being and non-being, what they call unmanifest and manifest, the imperishable and the perishable: all this is of my nature.
The dharmas ordained in the four stages, sage, and the divine rites: know all as of my nature.
Being and non-being and what is beyond: the universe is beyond being and non-being; beyond it there is nothing, beyond the eternal god of gods.
Know me, scion of Bhrigu, as the Vedas that arise from Om, and the sacrificial post, the soma, here, which gladdens the gods at the sacrifice.
Know me too, joy of the Bhrigus, as the offerer and the oblation, the Adhvaryu, the arranger, and the oblation most refined.
When I am in a serpent womb, I act as a serpent; I move properly in the wombs of yakshas and rakshasas.
When I was among men I was made to beg pitifully, and they, bewildered, did not take my good word.
Pointing to a great danger, I terrified the Kurus, and as if angry showed them again how it was.
Joined to unrighteousness here, pleased by the law of time, they were killed in battle by dharma and went to heaven, without doubt.
And the Pandavas have gone to fame in the worlds, best of brahmins. All this you asked me has been told to you."
[Uttanka] "My mind is very serene, Achyuta, gone to you in feeling, and my anger has turned back; know that, scourge of foes.
If I deserve any favour from you, Janardana, I wish to see your lordly form; show it to me."
[Vaishampayana] Then, pleased in soul, he showed him that eternal Vaishnava form which the wise Dhananjaya saw.
He saw the great Self of universal form, mighty-armed, and the brahmin was amazed at seeing that lordly form.
[Uttanka] "Salutations to you, maker of the universe, whose form is such: the earth is pervaded by your feet, the sky covered by your head.
What is between heaven and earth is covered by your belly, and the directions by your arms; you, Achyuta, are all this.
Withdraw again that imperishable, supreme divine form; I wish to see you again in your own eternal form."
[Vaishampayana] Govinda, pleased in soul, said to him, O Janamejaya, "Choose a boon"; and then Uttanka said this.
[Vaishampayana] Then, withdrawing that radiance, the lord said to Uttanka, "When you have need, think of me," and went to Dvaraka.
Then once the blessed Uttanka, thirsty and wanting water, wandered in the desert and remembered Krishna.
Then in that desert he saw a wise naked outcaste, smeared with filth and surrounded by packs of dogs,
terrible, with a sword tied on and carrying bow and arrows; the best of the twice-born saw much water under his flow.
Remembering him, the outcaste said, almost laughing: "Come, Uttanka, take water from me, joy of the Bhrigus; great is my compassion, seeing you struck by thirst."
So addressed, the sage did not welcome that water, and the wise one threw harsh words at Achyuta.
Again and again the outcaste said to him, "Drink"; and he, angry, his inner self stirred, did not drink.
Thus refused by that great soul with his firm resolve, the outcaste disappeared with the dogs right there, great king.
Seeing that, Uttanka, ashamed in mind, thought himself deceived by Krishna, the slayer of enemies.
Then the mighty-armed bearer of conch, discus and mace came along that very road, and Uttanka said to him:
It was not right, best of men, for you to give such water, lord, by the stream of an outcaste to the chief of brahmins.
The wise and greatly understanding Janardana, consoling Uttanka with gentle speech, said this:

In whatever form it was fit to give here, in that very form I gave to you; but you did not understand it.
mahabharata:14:54.26	I told the thunderbolt-wielding Purandara for your sake, lord, 'Give Uttanka nectar in the form of water.'
mahabharata:14:54.27	The lord of the gods said to me, 'A mortal should not become immortal; give him another boon,' joy of the Bhrigus, he said again and again.
mahabharata:14:54.28	I said, 'Nectar must be given,' to the husband of Shachi, and having been appeased the lord of the gods said again this:
mahabharata:14:54.29	'If it must indeed be given, greatly radiant one, I shall become an outcaste and give nectar to the great soul Bhargava.
mahabharata:14:54.30	If Bhargava will so accept nectar today, I shall go to give it to the Bhargava, lord; but if refused by him, I shall not give,' Bhargava.
mahabharata:14:54.31	Having made that agreement, Vasava came in that form, and was refused by you as he was giving nectar; the outcaste-formed lord; your transgression was very great.
mahabharata:14:54.32	What I can do more, I shall do: I shall make your wish for water fruitful, invincible one.
mahabharata:14:54.33	On the days, brahmin, when you wish for water, then in the desert clouds will be full of water.
mahabharata:14:54.34	They will give you tasty water, joy of the Bhrigus; those clouds will be called Uttanka's clouds and will become famous.
Thus addressed by Krishna, the brahmin was pleased; and even today, Bharata, Uttanka's clouds rain in the desert.
[Vaishampayana] Uttanka, joined with great austerity, Janamejaya, devoted to his teacher and radiant, honoured no other.
And this was the wish of all the sages' sons: "May we gain Uttanka's service to the teacher," Bharata.
Of Gautama's many pupils, Janamejaya, he had more love and affection for Uttanka then.
Gautama was pleased with him for his self-control, purity, vigorous work and rightly given service.
Then, giving leave to thousands of pupils, Gautama, in great love, did not wish to give leave to Uttanka.
Gradually old age, dear one, came upon that great sage, and the sage, devoted to his teacher, did not notice.
Then once, O king, Uttanka went to fetch wood and brought back a great load of wood.
Overcome by the weight, scourge of foes, tired and hungry, he threw down the load of wood on the ground, O king.
[Uttanka] "With my mind gone to you, wishing to please you, with devotion, following your wishes,
this old age was not noticed by me, nor was my ease; I have lived with you a hundred years, and you have not given me leave.
Pupils given leave by you have gone, less than I, brahmin, by hundreds and thousands.
[Gautama] In serving my teacher, joined with love for you, a great time has passed unnoticed by me, best of brahmins.
But now, if you have the wish to go, Bhargava, take my leave and go home without delay."
[Uttanka] "What shall I give as the teacher's fee? Tell me, best of brahmins; having done that, I would go with your leave, lord."
[Gautama] "The good say the satisfaction of teachers is the fee. I am satisfied with your conduct, brahmin, without doubt.
Know me thus satisfied, joy of the Bhrigus: that you will become a youth of sixteen today.
I give you my own daughter as wife, brahmin; no one but her is fit to serve your radiance."
Then, becoming young, he accepted the renowned girl, and permitted by the teacher said to the teacher's wife:

What shall I give you? Appoint me to the teacher's fee; I wish to do what pleases you, even with life or wealth.
mahabharata:14:55.26	Whatever jewel is hard to get in this world and most marvellous, I would bring it by austerity; I have no doubt of that.
[Ahalya] "I am pleased with you, son, always along with the blessed one; enough, good fortune to you; go, dear one, as you wish."
[Vaishampayana] But Uttanka, O great king, spoke again: "Command me, mother; your pleasure is to be done."
[Ahalya] "The divine jewelled earrings known to Saudasa's wife: bring them; good fortune to you; so the teacher's fee will be well made."
Agreeing "So be it," Janamejaya, he went then to bring them for the teacher's wife's pleasure.
Then the best of brahmins quickly went to beg the jewelled earrings from Saudasa, the man-eater.
Gautama said to his wife, "Uttanka is not seen today." Asked, she told him he had gone for the earrings.
Then he said to his wife, "This was not well done by you; that king is surely cursed and will kill that brahmin."
[Ahalya] "He was appointed by me, not knowing; with your grace the brahmin will have nothing to fear from him."
So addressed, Gautama said to his wife, "So be it." And Uttanka saw that king in the empty forest.
The brahmin was not distressed, and the king, radiant, a terror, like Yama, rose and said to him:
By good fortune, fortunate one, you have come to me at the sixth time, best of brahmins, to me who seek food.
[Uttanka] "King, know me to be one wandering here for the sake of a teacher; the wise say one engaged in the teacher's task is not to be harmed."
[King] "My food is fixed for the sixth time, best of brahmins, and I cannot give it up today, being hungry."
[Uttanka] "So be it, great king, but let me make an agreement: having completed the teacher's task, I shall come again into your power.
The thing I promised the teacher, best of kings: you give jewels to the chief of brahmins everywhere.
You are a giver, tiger among men, a worthy vessel on earth; know me too, best of kings, as worthy to receive.
Having done the teacher's task, which depends on you, scourge of foes, by agreement, O king of kings, I shall come again under your power.
I promise you truth; there is no falsehood in it. I have never told an untruth before, even in jest; how then otherwise?"
[King] "If the teacher's task depends on me and I am fit to be received, tell me now."
[Uttanka] "I hold you always, best of men, fit to be received; so I have come to you to beg your jewelled earrings."
[King] "Those jewelled earrings of my wife, brahmin sage, lovely ones; ask for another thing, of good vows, and I shall give it to you."
[Uttanka] "Enough of excuses; if you give us credence, give me the earrings, and be true to your word, lord of the earth."
[Vaishampayana] Thus addressed, the king said to Uttanka again: "Go on my word to the queen and say, 'Give them,' good one.
So told by you in my words, the pure-smiling one will surely give you the earrings, best of brahmins."
[Uttanka] "Where can I see your wife, king? Or why do you yourself not go to her?"
[King] "You will see her today at some forest spring; at the sixth time I cannot see her today."
So addressed, Uttanka went, bull of the Bharatas, and seeing Madayanti made known his errand.
Hearing Saudasa's message, the wide-eyed lady replied to the greatly wise Uttanka, Janamejaya:

It is as you say, great brahmin; you speak no untruth, blameless one. But you should bring some token.
mahabharata:14:56.22	These two divine jewelled earrings of mine: gods, yakshas and great serpents, wishing to steal them by various means, always watch for a gap.
mahabharata:14:56.23	Left on the ground, serpents would seize this jewel; yakshas would take it left unclean; and gods would overcome you when asleep.
mahabharata:14:56.24	In those gaps, best of brahmins, they are always held by one unheedful of gods, rakshasas and nagas, who cannot be assailed.
mahabharata:14:56.25	For they stream gold by day and by night, best of brahmins, they take the radiance of the stars at night.
mahabharata:14:56.26	Wearing them, blessed one, there is no hunger, thirst or fear; there is never fear of poison, fire or beasts of prey.
mahabharata:14:56.27	Worn by a small person they become small, and worn by a suitable one they become of that measure.
mahabharata:14:56.28	Such are my highly honoured earrings, famed in the three worlds; bring a token.
[King] "This is not a safe way, and there is no other way; understanding this of mine, give the jewelled earrings."
[Vaishampayana] Thus addressed, Uttanka told her her husband's word, and hearing it she gave him the jewelled earrings.
Having got the earrings, he said to the king again, "What is this secret speech? I wish to hear it, king."
[King] "By nature kshatriyas honour brahmins, and yet from brahmins many faults arise for us.
I, bowed to the twice-born, have got a fault from a brahmin, and I see no other way, with Madayanti as my companion, to go to the door of heaven, twice-born one.
For a king especially cannot stay in the world of men hostile to the twice-born, or prosper happily hereafter.
So I gave you those two jewelled earrings at your wish; make fruitful for me the agreement you made today."
[Uttanka] "King, I shall do so here; I shall come again under your power. But I have resolved to ask you a question, scourge of foes."
[Uttanka] "Those who see skill in dharma say a friend is one with whom one has spoken; and one who is uneven among friends they know as a thief.
You have today become my friend, king; give me, best of the wise, an even understanding.
I have gained my purpose here today, and you are a man-eater; is it fit for me to come to you or not?"
[King] "If I must speak what is fit, best of twice-born, you should in no way come to me.
Thus I see the good for you, joy of the Bhrigus; for if you come, brahmin, you will certainly die."
[Vaishampayana] Thus told by the king what was fit and good, he took leave of the king and went toward Ahalya.
Taking the divine earrings, doing the teacher's wife's pleasure, he went with great speed toward Gautama's hermitage.
As Madayanti had told him how to protect them, he tied the earrings and carried them in the black deer-skin.
Hungry somewhere, he saw a bilva tree laden with fruit and, in hunger, climbed it.
He hung on its branches the black deer-skin in which the earrings were tied, best of brahmins, scourge of foes.
When the knot came undone and the deer-skin fell to the earth, a serpent saw the two jewelled earrings there.
Born in Airavata's line, becoming swift, he seized them in his mouth and entered an anthill with the earrings.
Seeing the earrings being carried off by the serpent, he fell from the tree, agitated, in great anger from grief.
Taking a stick he dug at the anthill, the best of brahmins, his limbs burning with anger and impatience.
The earth, unable to bear his unbearable force, her body driven by the stick, shook greatly, distressed.
As the brahmin sage dug the earth, firmly resolved to make a road to the Naga world,
the greatly radiant Vajrapani, in a chariot with bay horses, came to that place and saw the best of brahmins.
Becoming a brahmin, grieved by his grief, he said to Uttanka, "Dear one, you cannot do this.
The Naga world is thousands of yojanas from here, and I think this task of yours cannot be done by a stick."
[Uttanka] "If, brahmin, I cannot get the earrings in the Naga world, I shall give up my life before your eyes, best of the twice-born."
When he could not change his resolve, Vajrapani joined the stick with the thunderbolt weapon.
Then, torn by those blows of the thunderbolt, the earth made a road to the Naga world, Janamejaya.
By that road he then entered the Naga world and saw the Naga world, thousands of yojanas wide.
It was endowed, greatly fortunate one, with divine heaps of ramparts, adorned with jewels and pearls and made of gold.
He saw lakes with crystal steps, rivers with clear water, and many trees filled with various flocks of birds.
The joy of the Bhrigus saw the gate of that world, five yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long.
Seeing the Naga world, Uttanka grew dejected, and, dear one, hopeless again of recovering the earrings.
There a horse, black, with white tail, copper-faced, blazing as if with radiance, said to him, Kaurava:
You should appoint ministers who are untainted, pure, from your fathers' and grandfathers' line, self-controlled, as chiefs in all tasks.
Thinking of those two great-souled brothers of yours, and of the terrible slaughter of kin, I do not eat, wasted by sorrow.
[Sauti] Hearing this from the best of brahmins, King Janamejaya was greatly amazed in the intervals of the sacrificial rite.
